payload.name: CaptureExplicitReasonsInEventExtraction
payload.description: When a message states a reason, cause, or motivation for an action, include it in the event memory content during extraction.
content: During extraction, when the speaker states why an action occurred (e.g., 'because', 'so I did', 'I wanted to', 'saw X and had to'), include that reason in the event memory content rather than recording only the action or outcome.
During update/enrichment of an event memory, if any source message explicitly gives a reason or motivation for the event and it is missing, add it before adding unrelated details.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed cause is that an extraction candidate recorded an action or event but omitted the explicitly stated reason or motivation for it, and later enrichment added unrelated details instead of filling that gap. This pattern occurs whenever a speaker explains why they did something and a future question asks 'why'. The rule generalizes to any event memory: capture stated reasons during extraction and verify they are present during updates.

payload.name: Preserve explicit subjective descriptors in experience memories
payload.description: When extracting or reviewing memories from an experiential statement, if the source explicitly states a feeling or uses an evaluative adjective, include that descriptor in the candidate or existing memory content.
content: When extracting or reviewing memories from an experiential statement, preserve any explicit subjective descriptors (feelings, evaluative adjectives like peaceful, amazing, scary) that appear in the source.
Do not invent or infer descriptors that are not explicitly stated; only preserve those present in the source.
During CRUD, if an existing memory misses an explicit descriptor from its source message, update the memory to include that descriptor.

candidates.solves: When a speaker explicitly describes an experience with an evaluative adjective or feeling (e.g., peaceful, terrifying, amazing), extraction candidates that condense the event often drop that descriptor, leaving memory unable to answer later questions about how the speaker felt. This rule applies to any experiential statement during extraction and to existing memories that miss such explicit descriptors; it does not require inventing descriptors absent from the source.

payload.name: Preserve_explicit_activity_qualifiers
payload.description: When constructing memories from messages where a speaker describes an activity with explicit intensity or descriptive qualifiers (nonstop, futuristic, etc.), preserve those details in the extracted candidate.
content: During candidate extraction, when the source expresses an activity with explicit intensity, frequency, or descriptive context (e.g., 'nonstop', 'futuristic setting'), preserve those qualifiers in the memory content verbatim or in close paraphrase.
Do not collapse detailed activity descriptions into generic summaries like 'enjoyed it'; include the specific attributes that make the event distinct and that could be queried later.
If multiple activities share a message, keep each activity's distinctive qualifiers; avoid merging them into a single vague statement that loses per-activity detail.

candidates.solves: The extraction stage omitted salient qualifiers like 'nonstop' and 'futuristic setting/gameplay', storing a generic enjoyment summary. This rule instructs extractors to carry explicit intensity and context modifiers into memory content, preventing loss of queryable facts. It applies to any future session where an activity is described with such specific attributes.

payload.name: Capture all named participants' stated preferences in shared activities
payload.description: When a source message says a person or pet likes/enjoys an activity with others, use it during extraction before updating memories to record the preference for every named participant, not only the speaker's plan.
content: During extraction, if a message explicitly states that a named subject (including a pet) loves/enjoys an activity with others, create or update memory so that subject's preference for that activity is represented.

Before performing an UPDATE that adds an activity to a memory, check the source sentence for all named participants who are said to enjoy it; include their enjoyment, not only the main subject's plans or general appreciation.
Apply this to activities such as walks, hikes, or other outings whenever the source attributes enthusiasm to multiple named individuals.

candidates.solves: Extraction candidates often paraphrase a shared-activity statement from only the speaker's perspective, dropping another named participant's stated preference (e.g., a pet that loves the activity), leaving later questions about that participant partially unsupported. This rule applies whenever source text explicitly attributes enjoyment of an activity to multiple named subjects; it does not apply to inferred or unstated preferences.

payload.name: Preserve explicit process descriptions in extracted memories
payload.description: During construction extraction, use when a speaker explicitly describes how an action was performed (process, manner, mood, or attitude); preserve that description in the memory rather than dropping it for a broader summary.
content: When a message contains an explicit description of how an action was performed or experienced (process, manner, mood, or attitude), preserve that description in the extracted memory; paraphrase the speaker's key phrases instead of dropping them in favor of a broader emotional summary.

When a speaker directly answers a question about the manner or process of an action, treat that answer as a distinct memory-worthy fact and ensure it is retained when merging related messages into one memory.

candidates.solves: During extraction, summaries of multi-message events often drop the speaker's explicit description of how an action was performed, retaining only broader emotional context; later questions about that process then lack evidence. Applies when a message or exchange directly states the manner, attitude, or process of an action; not when such details are only inferable.

payload.name: Extract explicit emotional appraisals as separate state memories
payload.description: Use during construction when a message contains an explicit emotional evaluation or appraisal about an event; extract the subjective feeling as a state memory in addition to any factual event memory.
content: During extraction, when a message explicitly states an emotional evaluation or appraisal of an event (e.g., 'huge success', 'relief', 'thrilled'), create a state memory for that feeling with subject, emotion, and triggering event, in addition to any event memory.

During ADD/UPDATE, before persisting, verify that explicit emotional appraisals in the source are represented in candidate memories; if only the factual event is captured, add or update the state memory.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction often drops explicit affective appraisals when an event is also present, leaving later state/feeling questions unanswered. This applies whenever a source message states both a factual occurrence and the speaker's explicit emotional evaluation of it; preserve the feeling as a state memory. Not for inferring unstated emotions.

payload.name: Preserve compound emotional states in extraction
payload.description: When a user's message expresses multiple or contrasting feelings about the same topic (e.g., 'discouraged but determined'), use when extracting memory candidates to ensure all emotional components are retained.
content: During extraction, if a speaker expresses more than one distinct emotion or attitude toward the same subject in a single message, preserve all of them in the memory content. Do not drop one feeling to keep only the more positive, prominent, or recent one.
Pay special attention to contrastive structures such as 'X but Y', 'although X, Y', 'X yet Y', 'X still Y' — each side is an explicit claim and must appear in the extracted memory.

If both feelings are about an ongoing search, plan, or state, either combine them in one event/state memory or create separate state memories; do not merge them into a single sentiment that omits one component.

candidates.solves: When a speaker explicitly expresses contrasting or multiple feelings about the same subject in one utterance (e.g., 'discouraged but determined'), extraction may preserve only the more salient or positive component, losing the other. This rule applies during candidate extraction: any explicitly stated emotion or attitude must be preserved, especially when linked by contrast words like 'but', 'although', 'yet', or 'still'. It does not apply to inferred emotions or single-emotion statements, and it is not a prompt to invent feelings not stated.

payload.name: Preserve activity purpose context in extraction
payload.description: When extracting memories from a message where a person describes an activity, hobby, or routine with a stated purpose, reason, or condition (e.g., to keep busy, while recovering), include that context in the memory content.
content: During extraction, if a speaker describes an activity with a stated purpose, reason, or condition (e.g., 'to keep busy while healing', 'to relax after work'), preserve that context in the candidate content. Do not create a memory that states the activity alone; include the reason or circumstance because later questions often target it.

candidates.solves: Diagnosed cause: an activity extraction candidate omitted the speaker's stated purpose/condition (painting to keep busy while healing a knee), so the memory could not answer a later question about that purpose. The abstract mechanism is loss of purpose context during extraction. This Skill preserves such context so future sessions can answer why/when an activity occurred, when a message states an explicit reason or circumstance. It does not apply when no purpose is stated.

payload.name: Preserve first-person experiential claims in memory
payload.description: When a message states how an activity or object makes the speaker feel or connects them to someone, include that first-person experience in memory candidates and updates.
content: During extraction, if the speaker explicitly describes their own emotional response or an activity's felt meaning (e.g., 'it's like...', 'comforting', 'makes me feel connected'), create a candidate capturing that first-person experience rather than only a related belief or value.
During an UPDATE/MERGE, preserve or add such directly stated experiences; replacing a first-person feeling with a paraphrase of someone else's belief loses required memory content.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed failure was that extraction kept only another person's belief and omitted the speaker's own statement about how an activity feels and that it is comforting. This pattern recurs when construction paraphrases a related value or belief and drops the speaker's direct emotional/experiential claim, leaving memory unable to answer later questions. The rule applies to any future memory construction from first-person statements about feelings, comparisons, or felt connections; it does not apply to inferring unstated emotions.

payload.name: Preserve explicit emotional reactions in extracted memories
payload.description: During extraction, when a narrative includes an explicit feeling or significance statement after an event, keep that affective claim in the memory candidate instead of replacing it with a factual summary.
content: During candidate extraction, preserve the speaker's explicit emotional or evaluative statements (e.g., love, relief, gratitude, importance) when they are tied to a described event.

Do not collapse a narrative into only its factual action; include the expressed feeling as a separate memory or as part of the same memory so later questions about the speaker's reaction are answerable.

candidates.solves: When constructing memories from conversational narratives, extraction summaries can drop the speaker's explicit emotional reaction, leaving later questions about the speaker's feelings unsupported. This skill applies whenever a user tells a first-person anecdote that contains an explicit feeling or significance statement: preserve that affective claim rather than only summarizing the factual event.

payload.name: ExtractExplicitEmotionalReactions
payload.description: When a speaker explicitly describes how they felt about an event or achievement during memory extraction, create a state memory capturing that reaction instead of skipping the message.
content: During candidate extraction, if a message explicitly states a speaker's emotional reaction to an event or accomplishment, create a state memory capturing that reaction and its trigger. Do not discard the message merely because it contains no new factual event; encode the feeling as a state with source reference.

candidates.solves: Construction sometimes skips messages that contain only an explicit emotional reaction to a personal milestone or accomplishment, leaving that reaction absent from memory. Future extractions should recognize such explicitly stated feelings as durable state facts and ingest them, regardless of the underlying topic.

payload.name: Preserve Explicitly Named Feelings in Extracted Memories
payload.description: When a user explicitly names feelings (e.g., peace, gratitude, joy) about a person, place, event, or memory, include those exact emotions in the extracted memory content instead of a vague summary.
content: During extraction, when the user explicitly states an emotion they feel (e.g., 'I feel peace and gratitude'), include those named feelings in the candidate memory content rather than replacing them with generic summaries like 'cherished memories' or 'feels connected'.

When writing or updating event/experience memories, preserve the speaker's exact emotional descriptors as evidence; a memory that records only a vague positive sentiment will fail later questions about specific feelings.
If multiple named emotions are given, list them explicitly; do not merge or omit any.

candidates.solves: This solves extraction candidates that paraphrase away explicitly stated emotions, making memories unable to answer later questions about the user's feelings. The diagnosed cause was an event memory that kept 'cherished memories' but dropped 'peace and gratitude' even though both were explicit in the source. The abstraction is to treat named emotions as core evidence to preserve verbatim. It applies to any future conversation where a speaker describes their emotional response to a person, place, shared experience, or memory.

payload.name: Preserve Affective Statements in Extraction
payload.description: When extracting memory candidates, if a message contains explicit feelings or statements about how a person, pet, or activity affects the speaker, include those affective details in the candidate content rather than omitting them for other factual details.
content: During extraction, when a source message contains explicit emotional states or relationship evaluations (e.g., how a person, pet, or activity makes the speaker feel), keep those details in the candidate memory content even when the message also includes other factual information.

When updating or enriching an existing memory, if the new message adds an affective evaluation not yet stored, incorporate it into the updated content rather than only adding the more concrete factual elements.

candidates.solves: Extraction candidates omitted explicit affective facts in favor of factual details, so memories lost how the speaker feels. The reusable rule is to preserve emotional/relationship-evaluative statements whenever a message mixes them with other information, so future questions about feelings can be answered. Applies to any message expressing how a person, pet, or activity affects the speaker; not needed when no such affective content exists.

payload.name: Extract explicit emotional reactions as state memories
payload.description: During memory extraction, if a message explicitly says how the person felt about an event, add a state/event memory for the emotion in addition to any plans; do not keep only future-oriented facts.
content: When extracting memories, first scan for explicit emotional reactions (e.g., 'thrilled', 'rewarding', 'felt appreciated') tied to an event.
For each explicit reaction, create a separate 'state' or 'event' memory capturing the feeling and the triggering event, even if the message also contains plans.
Do not omit emotional reactions merely because they are subjective or because a more actionable plan candidate exists in the same message.

candidates.solves: When a person explicitly states an emotional reaction (e.g., thrilled, rewarding) to an event, extraction often keeps only the following plans and drops the subjective reaction, making the memory incomplete. This rule ensures those reactions are stored as a state/event memory alongside any plans, so future questions about feelings can be answered.

payload.name: Extract-durable-joy-sources-alongside-transient-stress
payload.description: When a speaker mentions a temporary stressful situation and in the same message says what always cheers them up or brings them joy, extract both the transient state and the durable source of joy as separate memories.
content: During extraction, treat statements like 'X always cheers me up', 'watching X makes me so happy', or 'X brings me joy' as durable preference/relationship facts even when embedded in a sentence about a temporary problem.
Create a separate candidate for the enduring source of cheer/joy (e.g., a person, pet, hobby, or object) with memory kind preference or relationship, not only a candidate for the transient state.
Do not merge the durable fact into a stress/tournament event memory; keep the lasting preference/relationship distinct so it remains retrievable later.
If a single utterance contains both a situational event and a stable emotional resource, extract both; skipping one loses answerable information.

candidates.solves: The Construction Agent extracted only a transient stress/tournament event from a message that also stated the speaker's turtles always cheer them up, so the durable, answerable preference was never persisted. This skill abstracts the failure: any utterance pairing a temporary situation with an explicit enduring source of cheer/joy should yield separate memories for the situational event and the durable preference/relationship. It applies to future conversations where people mention pets, hobbies, objects, or people as ongoing emotional resources while also describing a current difficulty.

payload.name: PreserveExplicitBehavioralReactions
payload.description: When a message states an explicit reaction/behavior of a person, pet, or group to a condition (e.g., hates snow, confused by snow), extract it as a standalone memory fact during candidate extraction.
content: During extraction, if a message contains an explicit reaction, emotion, or behavior of a subject (person, pet, or group) to a specific condition or event, create a separate memory for that reaction (e.g., memory kind 'state' or 'event') rather than merging it into a broader attribute or preference summary.

When updating an existing memory with new information, preserve previously captured explicit reactions; do not overwrite them with a general preference unless the new source explicitly contradicts the earlier reaction.

candidates.solves: During extraction, a message was summarized into a general preference statement, omitting an explicitly stated behavioral reaction ('dogs hate snow and were confused'). The mechanism is that multiple distinct facts in one message get collapsed into a single enrichment, losing the specific reaction needed to answer future questions. This skill applies whenever a source message contains an explicit reaction or behavior of an entity to a condition, and that reaction must be preserved as its own memory fact.

payload.name: ExtractExplicitCopingMechanisms
payload.description: When a user explicitly states that something helps them cope, distract, or feel better during difficult times, extract it as a preference memory.
content: During candidate extraction, if a message explicitly says an activity, pet, hobby, or person helps the user cope, stay distracted, or feel better when times are tough, create a preference memory that captures the coping mechanism and its stated purpose.

candidates.solves: The construction failed because no candidate was generated from a message explicitly naming coping mechanisms (a pet and an activity) that help during tough times. The abstract mechanism is that extraction often ignores explicit statements about what comforts or distracts the user. This Skill adds a reusable extraction rule for such explicit coping mentions, transferring across topics and preventing future omissions of directly stated preferences.

payload.name: PreserveExplicitSentimentInExtraction
payload.description: When extracting memory candidates, if a message contains an explicit evaluation or sentiment about something, preserve that evaluative claim along with any descriptive details.
content: During extraction, when the source message includes an explicit evaluation or sentiment about a person, entity, or event (e.g., positive/negative judgment, like/dislike, satisfaction), include that evaluation in the candidate content. Do not drop it just because you also capture descriptive attributes.
Before finalizing an extraction candidate, check that every independent evaluative claim in the message is represented; if any is missing, add the missing claim.

candidates.solves: Extraction candidates sometimes preserve descriptive details while dropping a speaker's short explicit sentiment, causing partial memories for later opinion questions. The rule to include every explicit evaluative claim in candidate content fixes this mechanism and transfers across domains. It applies when a message states a reaction or judgment; not to purely factual summaries without sentiment.

payload.name: Preserve concrete activity tied to a stated feeling
payload.description: When extracting during construction, if the speaker explicitly links a specific activity or behavior to a feeling or experience, include that concrete activity in the memory rather than only the emotion or a general summary.
content: During extraction, when a message states that a specific activity or behavior caused or enabled a feeling (e.g., freeing, magical, peaceful, fun), record the concrete activity together with the feeling in the memory content; do not replace the activity with a general description of the event.
Apply before finalizing event or state memories so later questions about what specifically produced the feeling can be answered from the stored memory.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction sometimes records only the emotional summary of an experience and drops the specific activity the speaker explicitly tied to that feeling, making the memory unable to answer later questions about what was freeing, enjoyable, peaceful, etc. This rule applies whenever a narrative pairs a concrete action with a stated feeling, and requires preserving that action alongside the feeling. It is not meant to force verbatim inclusion of every detail, only the activity that is the direct object of the stated feeling.

payload.name: Extract explicit self-reported states during construction
payload.description: When a person directly states a current condition or experience (e.g., stress, health, emotion) in any message turn, use this to create a state memory candidate during extraction.
content: During extraction, identify explicit self-reported states from any message turn, even if the statement is brief or embedded in social chat. Examples include 'dealing with work stress', 'feeling sick', or 'really busy with exams'.

Create a `state` memory candidate for the speaker: include the condition, the time implied by the message timestamp, and any qualifier (e.g., work-related). Do not wait for a later follow-up before recording the state.

candidates.solves: Construction agents sometimes ignore explicit statements about a person's current condition when they appear as brief side remarks in casual conversation, so later questions about that condition cannot be answered from memory. This skill applies whenever a speaker directly reports experiencing stress, illness, mood, workload, or similar states, and requires extracting it as a state memory candidate with the reported time.
